Description: implicit — serverless tile hosting on GitHub Pages
prompt: I want to host map tiles on GitHub Pages without running any backend. Is that possible with MapLibre GL JS?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## Yes – you can serve **static PMTiles** from GitHub Pages and use them with MapLibre GL JS without any backend code. Below is a complete, step-by-step guide that covers: | What you’ll do | Why it matters | |----------------|----------------| | **Create or obtain a `.pmtiles` file** (vector, raster or raster-dem) | PMTiles is a single-file tile archive that MapLibre can read via HTTP range requests. | | **Make sure the file is ≤ 100 MiB** (GitHub Pages limit) | GitHub Pages only serves files up to 100 MiB; larger archives must be split or hosted elsewhere (e.g. S3, Cloudflare R2). | | **Upload the file to the `gh-pages` branch (or `docs/` folder)** | Anything in the published branch is served as a static asset. | | **Enable CORS & Range support** (GitHub Pages does this automatically) | MapLibre needs `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` to fetch tiles. | | **Add the PMTiles protocol handler to your MapLibre app** | MapLibre does not understand `.pmtiles` natively; the `pmtiles` library registers a `pmtiles://` protocol. | | **Reference the file in your style with `url:` (not `tiles:`)** | The protocol reads the archive header and supplies the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. | | **Deploy the site** | GitHub Pages will serve the HTML/JS and the `.pmtiles` file. | --- ## 1. Get a PMTiles file ### Option A – Convert an existing MBTiles file ```bash # Download the binary (Linux/macOS/Windows) from: # https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases pmtiles convert mytiles.mbtiles mytiles.pmtiles ``` ### Option B – Generate directly with tippecanoe (v2.17+) ```bash tippecanoe -zg -o mytiles.pmtiles mydata.geojson ``` ### Option C – Use a pre-built PMTiles set Protomaps offers ready-made basemaps (e.g. `protomaps-basemap-2024-09.pmtiles`). Download one that fits your size budget (most regional extracts are < 100 MiB). > **Size check** – Run `pmtiles show mytiles.pmtiles` and look at `tileCount` and `fileSize`. If it’s > 100 MiB you’ll need to: > * split the area (`pmtiles extract …`) or > * host the file on a CDN (S3, Cloudflare R2) and keep a tiny placeholder on GitHub Pages. --- ## 2. Add the file to a GitHub Pages repo 1. **Create (or use) a repository** that already has GitHub Pages enabled. - If you haven’t enabled Pages, go to **Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source** and select the `gh-pages` branch (or `main` + `/docs` folder). 2. **Copy the `.pmtiles` file** into the branch/folder that is published. ```bash # Example: using the /docs folder on the default branch mkdir -p docs/tiles cp mytiles.pmtiles docs/tiles/ git add docs/tiles/mytiles.pmtiles git commit -m "Add PMTiles archive" git push ``` 3. **Verify the file is reachable** (replace `USERNAME` and `REPO`): ``` https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/tiles/mytiles.pmtiles ``` Open that URL in a browser → you should see a download prompt or a raw binary view. **GitHub Pages automatically sends**: - `Accept-Ranges: bytes` - `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` No extra configuration is needed. --- ## 3. Install the PMTiles JavaScript library ```bash npm install pmtiles # or yarn add pmtiles ``` The library works with MapLibre GL JS v3-v6 and already contains a compatibility shim for the newer `addProtocol` signature. --- ## 4. Register the protocol **once** (e.g. in your app’s entry point) ```js // src/pmtiles-setup.js import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles'; import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; // Create a singleton protocol instance const pmtilesProtocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); // Register the handler globally maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', pmtilesProtocol.tile); // Optional clean-up (if you ever need to remove it) // export const removePmtilesProtocol = () => maplibregl.removeProtocol('pmtiles'); ``` > **Important:** Register *before* any `new maplibregl.Map()` is called. The registration is global, so you only need to do it once even if you mount many maps. --- ## 5. Build a MapLibre style that points at the hosted file ### Minimal example (vector tiles) ```js // src/map.js import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; import './pmtiles-setup'; // ensures protocol is registered const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', //
in your HTML style: { version: 8, sources: { // The URL is the GitHub Pages location of the .pmtiles file. // The `pmtiles://` prefix tells the protocol handler to use range requests. mytiles: { type: 'vector', url: 'pmtiles://https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/tiles/mytiles.pmtiles' } }, layers: [ { id: 'water', type: 'fill', source: 'mytiles', 'source-layer': 'water', // name of the layer inside the archive paint: { 'fill-color': '#a0c8f0' } }, { id: 'roads', type: 'line', source: 'mytiles', 'source-layer': 'road', paint: { 'line-color': '#777', 'line-width': 1 } } // add more layers as needed … ] }, center: [0, 0], zoom: 2 }); ``` ### Raster example (satellite imagery) ```json { "type": "raster", "url": "pmtiles://https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/tiles/satellite.pmtiles", "tileSize": 256, "maxzoom": 14 // optional – will be read from the archive header if omitted } ``` ### Raster-DEM (terrain) example ```json { "type": "raster-dem", "url": "pmtiles://https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/tiles/elevation.pmtiles", "encoding": "terrarium" } ``` Then enable terrain in the map: ```js map.setTerrain({ source: 'elevation', exaggeration: 1.5 }); ``` --- ## 6. Deploy the site If you’re using a static-site generator (Vite, Next static export, plain HTML, etc.) just push the built files to the branch that GitHub Pages serves. The `.pmtiles` file stays in the same repo, so the URL never changes. ```bash git add dist/ git commit -m "Deploy site" git push origin gh-pages # or whatever branch you configured ``` Visit `https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/` – the map should load instantly, fetching only the byte ranges it needs. --- ## 7. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---------|-------|-----| | **Map shows a blank background, no layers** | The source URL used `tiles:` instead of `url:`. | Use `url: 'pmtiles://…'`. The protocol reads the archive header and supplies the correct zoom range. | | **Console shows `Range header not supported`** | Hosting on a server that strips `Accept-Ranges`. | GitHub Pages supports it out-of-the-box. If you moved the file elsewhere, ensure the host returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. | | **CORS error** | The host does not send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. | GitHub Pages already sends `*`. For other hosts, configure CORS accordingly. | | **Tiles load up to a certain zoom then become empty** | The style used `tiles: ['…/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf']` which bypasses the archive’s `maxzoom`. | Switch to `url:` (as shown above). | | **`addProtocol` throws “callback is not a function”** | Using a MapLibre GL v4+ build with an old pmtiles handler (callback-style). | Use `new pmtiles.Protocol().tile` – it contains the v4 shim. Or upgrade `pmtiles` to ≥ 3.0.0. | | **File > 100 MiB and GitHub Pages refuses to serve it** | GitHub Pages size limit. | Split the archive (`pmtiles extract --bbox …`) or host the large file on a CDN (S3, Cloudflare R2) and reference that URL from the same GitHub Pages site. | | **Zoom levels beyond the archive’s max give “empty tiles”** | Using `tiles:` template or manually overriding `maxzoom`. | Keep `url:`; MapLibre will over-zoom automatically using the highest-available tiles. | --- ## 8. When you need more than one PMTiles file If your dataset is too big for a single file, you can: 1. **Create multiple regional archives** (e.g. `europe.pmtiles`, `asia.pmtiles`). 2. **Add a separate source for each** and use a **filter expression** to show the appropriate source only when the map is inside its bounds: ```json { "id": "roads-europe", "type": "line", "source": "europe", "source-layer": "road", "filter": ["all", [">=", ["zoom"], 5], ["within", ["bbox", [ -10, 35, 30, 70 ]]]] } ``` Or, more simply, **use Martin** (a tiny Node server) that can merge multiple PMTiles files on the fly and still be deployed as a static binary behind a CDN. For most small-to-medium projects a single file is enough. --- ## 9. Full minimal repository layout (example) ``` my-map/ ├─ public/ │ ├─ index.html │ └─ tiles/ │ └─ mytiles.pmtiles ← uploaded to GitHub Pages ├─ src/ │ ├─ pmtiles-setup.js │ └─ map.js ├─ package.json └─ vite.config.js (or any bundler you like) ``` **`index.html`** ```html PMTiles on GitHub Pages
``` Deploy with: ```bash npm run build # produces ./dist git add dist git commit -m "Deploy" git push origin gh-pages ``` Now `https://USERNAME.github.io/my-map/` shows the map powered entirely by a static PMTiles file. --- ## 10. TL;DR checklist 1. **Create/convert** a `.pmtiles` file (≤ 100 MiB for GitHub Pages). 2. **Commit** it to the branch/folder that GitHub Pages serves. 3. **Add the `pmtiles` JS library** and register `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', …)`. 4. **Reference the file with `url: 'pmtiles://https://…/mytiles.pmtiles'`** in your style. 5. **Deploy** the site – GitHub Pages handles CORS and Range requests automatically. That’s it – you now have a completely server-less map stack: static HTML/JS + a single PMTiles archive hosted on GitHub Pages. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a quick, **zero-install-if-you-already-have the binary** checklist you can run locally to be 100 % sure the `.pmtiles` archive is:

* a valid PMTiles file (no corruption, correct offsets, etc.)
* contains the vector layers you expect (or the raster band you expect)
* has the right zoom range, bounds and metadata before you push it to S3 / R2 / GitHub Pages.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the official **pmtiles CLI** (once)

| OS | Command |
|----|---------|
| macOS (brew) | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` |
| Linux/macOS (curl) | `curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/latest/download/pmtiles-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m) -o pmtiles && chmod +x pmtiles && sudo mv pmtiles /usr/local/bin/` |
| Windows (PowerShell) | `iwr https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/latest/download/pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe -OutFile pmtiles.exe` (add the folder to `PATH`) |
| Docker (no install) | `docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/data protomaps/go-pmtiles:latest <sub-command>` |

> **Tip:** The binary is a single ~5 MB file, no runtime dependencies. If you already have Docker, the Docker line is the fastest way to try it without touching your host.

---

## 2️⃣ Verify the archive is *structurally* sound

```bash
pmtiles verify my-tiles.pmtiles
```

*What you’ll see*  

```
✔︎ Header checksum OK
✔︎ Tile index checksum OK
✔︎ All tile offsets are within file bounds
✔︎ No duplicate tile entries
```

If anything fails you’ll get an error line (e.g. “tile offset out of range”). In that case regenerate the archive – the CLI can’t fix a corrupted file.

---

## 3️⃣ Peek at the **header & TileJSON** (includes layer list for vector tiles)

```bash
pmtiles show my-tiles.pmtiles
```

Typical output for a **vector** PMTiles file:

```
File: my-tiles.pmtiles
Version: 2
Tile type: vector
Bounds: -180.0,-85.0511,180.0,85.0511
Zoom range: 0-14
Tile count: 1 234 567
TileJSON:
{
  "tilejson": "3.0.0",
  "name": "my-tiles",
  "bounds": [-180,-85.0511,180,85.0511],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "center": [0,0,2],
  "vector_layers": [
    {"id":"water","description":"","minzoom":0,"maxzoom":14},
    {"id":"roads","description":"","minzoom":5,"maxzoom":14},
    {"id":"places","description":"","minzoom":8,"maxzoom":14}
  ]
}
```

*Key things to check*

| Field | Why it matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **Tile type** | `vector`, `raster` or `raster-dem`. If you expected vector but see `raster`, you generated the wrong kind. |
| **Bounds** | Must cover the area you intend to serve. |
| **Zoom range** | `minzoom`/`maxzoom` are taken from the header; MapLibre will over-zoom automatically if you use `url:` (see the skill). |
| **vector_layers** (or `raster_layers` for raster) | The exact `id` strings you will use in `"source-layer": "<id>"` in your style. If a layer you need is missing, you have to regenerate the archive with the proper source data. |

> **Note:** `pmtiles show` prints the *TileJSON* that the protocol handler will hand to MapLibre when you use `url:`. If you see an empty `vector_layers` array, the file is probably a raster archive or you generated MBTiles without a TileJSON (some older tippecanoe versions did that). Regenerate with `--layer` flags or upgrade tippecanoe ≥ 2.17.

---

## 4️⃣ (Optional) Inspect a **single tile** to double-check layer contents

Sometimes you want to be absolutely sure the geometry inside a tile is what you expect (e.g. after a custom Planetiler build). The CLI can dump a tile as raw PBF, then you can decode it with any vector-tile viewer.

### 4.1 Dump a tile

```bash
# Choose a zoom that you know contains data, e.g. z=10, x=512, y=384
pmtiles tile my-tiles.pmtiles 10 512 384 > tile.pbf
```

### 4.2 Decode the PBF (Node, Python, or CLI)

**Node (quick-look)**

```bash
npm install -g @mapbox/vector-tile vt2geojson
vt2geojson tile.pbf | jq '.features[].properties.layer' | sort -u
```

**Python (if you prefer)**

```python
pip install mapbox-vector-tile
import json, mapbox_vector_tile
with open("tile.pbf","rb") as f:
    tile = mapbox_vector_tile.decode(f.read())
print(json.dumps(tile.keys(), indent=2))
```

You’ll get a list like:

```
[
  "water",
  "roads",
  "places"
]
```

If the list matches the `vector_layers` you saw in `pmtiles show`, you’re good to go.

---

## 5️⃣ Quick “one-liner” sanity check (combine steps)

If you just want a single command that tells you *“valid + layer list”*:

```bash
pmtiles verify my-tiles.pmtiles && pmtiles show my-tiles.pmtiles | grep -A5 '"vector_layers"'
```

If the `verify` part exits with a non-zero status the script will stop, so you’ll never trust a broken file.

---

## 6️⃣ What to do if something is wrong

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| `pmtiles verify` reports “tile offset out of range” | Corrupted file (e.g. incomplete upload, disk error) | Regenerate the archive; if you used `pmtiles convert`, make sure the source MBTiles is not corrupted (`mbtiles verify` if you have it). |
| `pmtiles show` shows **no `vector_layers`** | You generated a raster archive, or used an old tippecanoe version that omitted TileJSON. | Regenerate with `tippecanoe -o out.pmtiles --layer=roads --layer=water …` (v2.17+). |
| Layer names are different from what you expected | Your source data used different layer names, or you passed `--layer` flags that renamed them. | Re-run the tile generator with the correct `--layer` or `--output-layer` options, or edit the TileJSON with `pmtiles edit` (see CLI docs). |
| Bounds are too large / too small | The source data’s extent was clipped, or you passed `--bounds` incorrectly. | Regenerate with the proper `--bounds` (tippecanoe) or `--bbox` (Planetiler). |
| Zoom range is off (e.g. maxzoom = 22 but you only have tiles up to 14) | You built the archive with a high `--maxzoom` but didn’t actually generate tiles that high. | Either generate the missing zoom levels or lower `maxzoom` in the TileJSON (`pmtiles edit --maxzoom 14`). |

---

## 7️⃣ Upload-ready checklist

1. **File size** – Make sure the final `.pmtiles` is under any static-host limit (GitHub Pages ≈ 100 MiB, Netlify ≈ 100 MiB, S3/R2 have no practical limit).  
2. **CORS headers** – `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) and `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. Most CDNs add these automatically, but you can set them on S3 with `aws s3api put-object-acl … --grant-read uri="http://acs.amazonaws.com/groups/global/AllUsers"` and `aws s3api put-object --bucket … --key … --metadata-directive REPLACE --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000"`.  
3. **Cache-Control** – Long-term caching (`public, max-age=31536000`) is recommended because the file is immutable.  
4. **Test the live URL** – After upload, run a quick fetch from your terminal to confirm range support:

   ```bash
   curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/my-tiles.pmtiles
   ```

   You should see `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and a `206 Partial Content` response.

5. **MapLibre quick test** – Spin up a tiny HTML page (or use the official example) that registers the protocol and points to the live URL. If the map renders the expected layers, you’re done.

---

## 8️⃣ TL;DR – One-page cheat sheet

```bash
# 1️⃣ Install (once)
brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles   # macOS
# or curl … (see above)

# 2️⃣ Verify integrity
pmtiles verify my-tiles.pmtiles

# 3️⃣ Show header + layer list
pmtiles show my-tiles.pmtiles

# 4️⃣ (Optional) Look at a single tile
pmtiles tile my-tiles.pmtiles 10 512 384 > tile.pbf
vt2geojson tile.pbf | jq '.features[].properties.layer' | sort -u
```

If **both commands succeed** and the `vector_layers` array contains the names you plan to use in your style, you can safely upload the file to any static host that supports HTTP range requests.

Happy mapping! 🚀

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR You used a **`tiles:`** array (`pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) instead of a **`url:`** property. When MapLibre reads a `tiles:` source it **does not look inside the PMTiles archive** for the min-/max-zoom values that are stored in the file header. So MapLibre assumes the default `maxzoom: 22` (and `minzoom: 0`). At zoom levels that are **higher than the archive actually contains**, the PMTiles protocol still receives the request, but the archive has no tile for that zoom → it returns an empty tile → you see a blank map. The fix is to reference the archive with **`url:`** (or, if you really need a `tiles:` template, explicitly set `maxzoom`/`minzoom` to the values that the archive reports). Below is a full explanation of why this happens, how to verify the correct zoom range, and the exact steps to make it work again. --- ## 1. What the `url:` vs `tiles:` properties do | Property | What MapLibre expects | What the PMTiles protocol does | |----------|----------------------|--------------------------------| | **`url`** (TileJSON) | A single URL that points to a *TileJSON* document (or, for PMTiles, a special handler that reads the archive header). | The `pmtiles` protocol opens the `.pmtiles` file, reads its **header**, and returns a TileJSON object that already contains `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, `center`, etc. MapLibre then knows the exact zoom range that the archive supports and will **over-zoom** automatically when you ask for a higher zoom. | | **`tiles`** (template) | An array of URL templates that MapLibre will fill with `{z}/{x}/{y}` and request directly. | The protocol treats each request as a plain HTTP fetch of a tile. It **does not read the archive header** first, so MapLibre never learns the archive’s native zoom range. It falls back to the default `maxzoom: 22`. If you request a zoom that the archive does not contain, the protocol returns a *null* tile → blank. | ### Why `url:` is the recommended way for PMTiles * The PMTiles file already knows its own zoom range (e.g. `minzoom: 0`, `maxzoom: 14`). * The protocol can return a **TileJSON** that includes those values, so MapLibre can: * Stop requesting tiles that don’t exist. * Over-zoom gracefully (re-use the highest-available tiles) instead of showing blanks. * You only need **one line** in the style (`url: "pmtiles://https://example.com/tiles.pmtiles"`). No need to write a `{z}/{x}/{y}` template. --- ## 2. What you observed 1. **`pmtiles show myfile.pmtiles`** prints something like: ``` minzoom: 0 maxzoom: 14 bounds: [-180,-85,180,85] tile count: 1 234 567 ``` 2. In the style you wrote: ```json "sources": { "mytiles": { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/myfile.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"] } } ``` 3. At zoom ≤ 14 everything works (tiles are served from the archive). 4. At zoom 15+ the map goes blank. **Root cause:** MapLibre thinks the source can serve up to zoom 22 (the default). It asks the PMTiles protocol for tile z=15, x=…, y=…. The archive has no entry for zoom 15, so the protocol returns `null`. MapLibre draws a blank tile. --- ## 3. How to fix it ### 3.1. Use the `url:` property (the simplest, most robust) ```json { "sources": { "mytiles": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/myfile.pmtiles" } } } ``` *No `tiles:` array at all.* When the map starts, the PMTiles protocol reads the header, returns a TileJSON that contains the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, and MapLibre will automatically over-zoom beyond `maxzoom` (re-using the highest-resolution tiles) instead of showing blanks. ### 3.2. If you *must* keep a `tiles:` template (rare) Add explicit `minzoom` and `maxzoom` that match the archive: ```json { "sources": { "mytiles": { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/myfile.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 // <-- match the archive header } } } ``` Now MapLibre will stop requesting zoom 15+ and will over-zoom automatically (it will reuse the zoom-14 tiles). **Caveat:** You have to keep these numbers in sync with the archive whenever you rebuild it. Using `url:` avoids that maintenance burden. ### 3.3. Verify the fix 1. Reload the page. 2. Open the browser dev-tools → **Network** → filter for `pmtiles://…`. 3. You should see only requests for zoom levels that exist in the file (e.g. `z=0…14`). 4. Zoom beyond the max; the map should still display (over-zoomed) instead of turning blank. --- ## 4. Quick checklist for a healthy PMTiles setup | ✅ Item | Why it matters | |--------|----------------| | **Protocol registration** – `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', new pmtiles.Protocol().tile)` – done **once** before any map is created. | Without it the `pmtiles://` scheme is unknown. | | **Source uses `url:`** (or `tiles:` + explicit `maxzoom`). | Guarantees correct zoom range. | | **CORS & Range support** on the host (S3, R2, GitHub Pages, etc.). | The client must be able to request byte ranges. | | **Cache-Control** header on the `.pmtiles` file (e.g. `public, max-age=31536000`). | CDN and browser cache the file efficiently. | | **`pmtiles show`** matches the zoom range you expect. | Confirms the archive is correct before uploading. | | **If you split the world into multiple files**, add a *source selector* (e.g. `source: 'tiles-europe'` vs `tiles-asia`) or use a custom source that switches based on map bounds. | Prevents a single gigantic file from becoming a bottleneck. | --- ## 5. Example: Full minimal MapLibre + PMTiles setup ```html PMTiles demo
``` *If you really need a `tiles:` array, just add `"maxzoom": 14` (or whatever `pmtiles show` reports) to the source definition.* --- ## 6. Common follow-up questions | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **What if I want different zoom limits for different layers?** | The zoom limits are **per source**, not per layer. If you need different limits, create separate sources (each pointing to its own PMTiles file or the same file with a different `maxzoom` override). | | **Can I mix `url:` and `tiles:` in the same source?** | No. The style spec allows **either** `url` **or** `tiles`. Using both is undefined and will be ignored. | | **My archive contains raster tiles – does the same rule apply?** | Yes. Whether `type: 'raster'` or `type: 'raster-dem'`, you still reference it with `url:`. The zoom-range issue is identical. | | **I’m using React and create the map in a component – where should I register the protocol?** | Register it **once** at the top level of your app (e.g. in `index.js` or a custom hook that runs only on the first render). Doing it inside each component can cause duplicate registrations or race conditions. | | **I see “Range Not Satisfiable” errors in the network tab after the fix.** | Double-check that the host returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. Some static hosts (e.g., older Netlify builds) strip that header; enable it or switch to a host that supports range requests (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages). | --- ## 7. Bottom line *Using a `tiles:` array bypasses the PMTiles header, so MapLibre assumes the default max-zoom (22). When you zoom past the archive’s native max-zoom, the protocol returns empty tiles → blank map.* **Solution:** Switch to `url:` (or explicitly set `maxzoom`/`minzoom` to match the archive). After that, the map will continue to display (over-zoomed) correctly at any zoom level. Happy mapping! 🚀
